lead: A heart-rate monitor turns an ECG into a beat count and a number on a screen. It detects each QRS complex, times the RR interval, and displays beats per minute. A Holter monitor records the same ECG for a whole day so a doctor can replay it later. Both depend on clean electrodes, a stable amplifier, and quick fault finding. You meet them in bedside monitors, 24-hour cardiac checks, and home ECG patches.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.1 for the action potential and Chapter 1.5 for ECG leads and display.

sections.h3: Heart-rate monitor: from QRS to bpm

blocks.text: A heart-rate monitor starts with surface ECG electrodes. The bio-amplifier removes common-mode voltage and raises the millivolt ECG to a usable level. The QRS detector then marks the sharp ventricular depolarisation. It does not count every P wave or T wave. From each mark, an RR timer measures the time to the next mark.

items: Band-pass filter the ECG to about 5–15 Hz, the usual QRS band, to keep QRS energy and reject baseline wander and high-frequency noise.
Use slope or threshold detection to find a QRS. A short refractory window, such as 200 ms, stops double counting.
Time the interval between two QRS marks; this is the RR interval.
Convert RR to rate and update the display and alarm limits.

blocks.where: HR<sub>inst</sub> is instantaneous heart rate in beats per minute; RR is the interval between two QRS complexes in seconds; 60 changes seconds to minutes.

blocks.text: Averaged heart rate is more stable for display: HR<sub>avg</sub> = N<sub>QRS</sub> ÷ t<sub>min</sub>. Here N<sub>QRS</sub> is the number of QRS complexes and t<sub>min</sub> is the total time in minutes. A monitor sounds an alarm when the rate crosses limits set by the clinician. Arrhythmia alarms and foetal monitoring belong to Unit 2.

sections.h3: Holter monitor: a full-day ECG record

blocks.text: A Holter monitor is a small battery recorder worn for 24 h or more. Chest electrodes feed the same kind of ECG amplifier, but the output goes to memory instead of only a screen. Older recorders used cassette tape; modern ones use flash memory. The record holds every ECG sample with a time stamp, so short events are not missed.

The patient keeps a diary and may press an event button when symptoms occur. At replay, software scans the whole record. It finds QRS complexes, plots heart rate against time, and shows full ECG around events. A doctor reads the replay to link symptoms with the rhythm. Average heart rate for the record uses total QRS complexes divided by total minutes.

items: Cassette or flash memory stores the full ECG; flash is common now because it has no moving parts.
Replay software marks QRS events, trends RR intervals and finds pauses or rate changes.
Event markers and diary times guide the doctor to the important strips.

blocks.text: Troubleshooting separates four fault groups: patient, electrode, cable or amplifier, and interference. Start by looking at the raw ECG, not only the heart-rate number. A clean QRS with a bad rate number points to the detector or settings. A poor ECG points to electrodes, cable or interference.

Reseat electrode, check gel and cable

blocks.text: Routine checks keep the recorder honest. On a paper ECG machine, apply a 1 mV calibration pulse and confirm 10 mm deflection at standard gain, then check paper speed at 25 mm/s. On a Holter, check sampling rate, channel count, clock and date-time, battery and the event button. Clean electrodes and cables; replace dried gel. Test each lead for lead off and cable break.

examples.question: A 24-hour Holter record contains 108,000 QRS complexes. Find the average heart rate in beats per minute.
steps: Average heart rate = total QRS complexes ÷ total minutes.
Average heart rate = 108,000 ÷ 1440 = 75.0 beats per minute.
examples.answer: The average heart rate is 75 beats per minute (bpm).
examples.check:
beats = 108000
hours = 24
minutes = hours * 60
average_hr = beats / minutes
print(average_hr)

traps: Average heart rate divides total QRS complexes by total minutes, not total hours. Dividing by 24 h instead of 1440 min gives 4,500 beats per hour, which is not a rate in bpm; convert hours to minutes first so the answer comes out as 75 bpm.
Instantaneous heart rate is 60 ÷ RR with RR in seconds. If RR is given in milliseconds, divide by 1000 first.
The QRS detector counts QRS complexes, not P waves or T waves. A high count can come from muscle noise or from double-counting one beat.

50 Hz interference gives a thick fuzzy trace at mains frequency; baseline wander is a slow swing from respiration or sweat; muscle artefact is high-frequency spikes. Do not label all three as the same fault.
A Holter total of 108,000 QRS complexes over 24 h is an average rate, not the peak rate. Do not report it as a maximum.

quiz.q: What does the QRS detector in a heart-rate monitor count?
quiz.a: It counts QRS complexes, which mark ventricular depolarisation, and ignores P and T waves.

quiz.q: Why does a heart-rate monitor use a refractory period after each detected QRS?
quiz.a: It stops one QRS from being counted twice and reduces false counts from T waves or noise.

quiz.q: An RR interval is 0.75 s. Find instantaneous heart rate.
A 12-hour Holter record has 54,000 QRS complexes. Find average heart rate.
An ECG trace shows a normal QRS but a thick fuzzy line at 50 Hz. What is the likely fault and what do you check?
quiz.a: Likely mains interference; check electrode contact, cable shielding, ground and nearby equipment.

quiz.q: What causes slow baseline wander in an ECG?
quiz.a: Respiration, sweat, electrode movement and poor skin preparation; a high-pass filter reduces it.

quiz.q: A monitor shows 150 bpm but many small spikes appear between QRS complexes. Give two checks before accepting the value.
quiz.a: Check electrode placement and skin for muscle artefact; adjust QRS threshold and refractory period, and verify the rate on the raw ECG. If a true arrhythmia is present, refer to Unit 2.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern patches record ECG for days and send it over a phone link. Software can scan a Holter record and mark suspected events, but a doctor still checks the ECG. Search for wearable ECG, Holter analysis and QRS detection if you want the next step.
